  - heading "What it is" [level=2]
  - paragraph: AI Project Pack is a public, single-repository operating pack for AI-assisted development. It gives a project one durable operating surface so a new AI session does not have to guess what is true, what is unresolved, and what should happen next.
  - paragraph: The product is the repository itself. This page exists to explain that repository clearly before you open GitHub.
  - paragraph: It is not a memory service, not an autonomous manager, and not a hosted platform. It is a reviewable text-first operating repo.
  - heading "Why it exists" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Projects drift when decisions stay trapped in chat, unresolved items get treated as settled, sources are not visible, and each new model session has to reconstruct context again from scratch.
  - paragraph: "AI Project Pack fixes that by separating the work into explicit, durable files:"
  - list:
    - listitem: current truth
    - listitem: decisions
    - listitem: pending items
    - listitem: next actions
    - listitem: sources
    - listitem: append-only update logs
  - heading "Who it is for" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Use it when project quality drops because context keeps resetting between AI sessions.
  - list:
    - listitem: product and technical planning with iterative AI support
    - listitem: research-heavy implementation where evidence quality matters
    - listitem: OSS release preparation with model handoff across sessions
    - listitem: mixed human + AI teams that need auditable changes
  - paragraph: It is a poor fit if you want autonomous project management or a platform that stores and runs work for you.
  - heading "What is inside the repository" [level=2]
  - paragraph: The repository is organized so AI can read, reason, and update within a visible operating surface instead of relying on hidden context.

    - heading "Important note" [level=2]
    - paragraph: This page and repository are workflow aids for repository-based development. They do not replace code review, testing, security review, release ownership, legal review, SLA review, or human release decisions.
    - paragraph: Before using any output in a real release, review the diff, run tests, confirm permissions, and check customer or production impact.
  - heading "What it is" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Codex Product Shipping Playbooks is a practical workflow guide for repository-based development. It is built for change work inside real codebases, where teams need more than a vague implementation idea or a generic project-management template.
  - paragraph: "This repository helps turn “we want this change” into a structured path: scope the change, define the delta, plan the implementation, set acceptance criteria, check readiness, write release artifacts, review the diff, and capture what was learned."
  - paragraph: It is not a release guarantee, a prompt pack, a broad PM framework, or a substitute for responsible engineering review. It is a repository-first guide for organizing real change work around code.
  - heading "Who it is for" [level=2]
  - paragraph: This project is a good fit for people who work with existing repositories and want a clearer path from change request to release. It is especially useful if you want acceptance criteria, pre-ship review, release writing, and retrospective work to connect back to the original change instead of living as disconnected documents.
  - list:
    - listitem: Teams using Codex or agent-assisted development on top of an existing repository.
    - listitem: Builders who want spec delta, planning, acceptance, and shipping steps to be explicit.
    - listitem: People who want release notes, changelog entries, and diff review to be part of the same operational loop.
    - listitem: Anyone who prefers reusable working assets over abstract workflow advice.
  - paragraph: It is a worse fit if you are looking for a general PM framework, a GTM library, or a catch-all prompt pack for unrelated tasks.
  - heading "The workflow path" [level=2]
  - paragraph: The current core path is built as a sequence that starts with repository understanding and ends with post-ship learning. The goal is to reduce ambiguity at each stage and create a repeatable issue-to-release loop.
  - strong: 1. intake-repo
  - text: Understand the repository before proposing work. Establish relevant files, routes, state layers, and likely impact areas.
  - strong: 2. spec-delta
  - text: Define the delta between current behavior and intended behavior so the change is framed precisely.
  - strong: 3. plan-change
  - text: Turn the delta into a concrete implementation plan that can guide real repository work.
  - strong: 4. define-acceptance
  - text: State what counts as done before the work is declared complete.
  - strong: 5. ship-check
  - text: Run practical pre-ship checks so readiness is not treated as a vague feeling.
  - strong: 6. write-release-artifacts
  - text: Prepare release-facing outputs such as release notes and changelog entries.
  - strong: 7. review-diff
  - text: Review the implemented diff against the intended change and what was actually delivered.
  - strong: 8. post-ship-retro
  - text: Capture lessons after shipping so future changes improve from concrete experience.
  - heading "What’s included" [level=2]
  - paragraph: The repository is organized around reusable layers that make the system easier to apply across multiple changes instead of rebuilding the workflow from scratch each time.
  - heading "Playbooks" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Concrete workflow units for repo intake, spec delta work, planning, acceptance definition, shipping checks, release writing, implementation review, and retrospective work.
  - heading "Artifacts" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Reusable templates for outputs such as spec deltas, change plans, acceptance definitions, release notes, changelog entries, diff reviews, and retrospectives.
  - heading "Gates" [level=3]

  - heading "What it is" [level=2]
  - paragraph: "codex-work-os is a practical work-system repository for Codex. It is built for situations where information arrives in fragments: loose meeting notes, partial research, half-formed support cases, unclear ownership, and unfinished reply drafts."
  - paragraph: The goal is not to make Codex sound more confident. The goal is to help Codex turn unstructured work into reviewable drafts and structured artifacts such as sales replies, PM briefs, executive summaries, decision memos, and support escalations.
  - paragraph: This repository is not primarily a prompt pack, not a generic PM framework, and not a random business templates library. It is a Codex-native operating layer for structured work.
  - heading "Who it is for" [level=2]
  - paragraph: This project is a strong fit for people who want Codex to help with operational work beyond coding and who prefer reusable working structure over one-off prompting.
  - list:
    - listitem: People who want sales, PM, research, executive, or support outputs to follow a stable shape.
    - listitem: Teams using Codex in workflows where information is messy and work products need review before use.
    - listitem: Builders who want flows, gates, and output types to be explicit rather than implied.
    - listitem: Anyone who wants AI outputs that are easier to review, hand off, adapt, or archive.
  - paragraph: It is a weaker fit if you are looking for a broad life-assistant prompt pack, a generic business advice library, or a coding-only helper repository.
  - heading "The five core packs" [level=2]
  - article:
    - heading "sales-pack" [level=3]
    - paragraph: For inquiry triage, proposal prep, and sales reply drafts that need review before sending.
  - article:
    - heading "pm-pack" [level=3]
    - paragraph: For status briefs, blocker maps, weekly updates, and decision-oriented progress summaries.
  - article:
    - heading "exec-assist-pack" [level=3]
    - paragraph: For short, high-signal briefs intended to support leaders and decision-makers.
  - article:
    - heading "research-pack" [level=3]
    - paragraph: For comparison work, decision memos, evidence summaries, and trade-off-based recommendations for review.
  - article:
    - heading "cs-pack" [level=3]
    - paragraph: For support summaries, escalation notes, and clearer handoffs for the next owner.
  - heading "How it is structured" [level=2]
  - paragraph:

    - code: skills/

  - heading "What it is" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - code: product-founder-os
    - text: "is a practical repository asset for product development with GPT and/or Codex. Its job is not to produce one-shot output and disappear. Its job is to give product work a durable structure: what you are building, what changed, what comes next, and what is actually done."
  - paragraph: AI-assisted product work often breaks in familiar ways. Implementation starts before the product is properly defined. Docs drift away from what is actually being built. Scope changes happen in conversation but never make it into the repository. “Done” gets claimed long before completion is real. This repository exists to reduce that drift by treating files such as project seed, product brief, functional spec, roadmap, current sprint, change requests, and done definition as source-of-truth operating files.
  - heading "Who it is for" [level=2]
  - paragraph: This repository is for people who want to build products with GPT and/or Codex across multiple sessions without losing coherence.
  - list:
    - listitem: Solo builders starting from a vague product idea
    - listitem: People planning a small SaaS or static tool before implementation
    - listitem: Repositories that already have code but weak product definition
    - listitem: Projects that need explicit scope handling and change tracking
    - listitem: Builders who want to know what is truly done and what is still open
  - paragraph: It is less suitable if you only want a tiny one-off script immediately, or if you want to skip planning entirely and jump straight into code.
  - heading "What it does" [level=2]
  - heading "Turns vague ideas into working product docs" [level=3]
  - paragraph: It helps organize project seed, product brief, target user, problem, scope, and non-goals into a usable starting point.
  - heading "Connects specs to planning" [level=3]
  - paragraph: It gives the repository a functional spec, roadmap, task backlog, current sprint, and done definition so implementation has a real baseline.
  - heading "Makes change visible" [level=3]
  - paragraph:
    - code: change-requests.md
    - text: makes requirement changes explicit and encourages updating docs before changing implementation direction.
  - heading "Checks the foundation" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Helper scripts can check baseline doc presence, markdown link integrity, stable content leakage, and malformed code fences.
  - heading "Modes" [level=2]
  - heading "Discover" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Figure out what should be built and turn that into a usable starting point.
  - heading "Define" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Clarify the product, the user, the problem, the scope, and the intended behavior.
  - heading "Plan" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Turn the current definition into milestones, backlog items, and an executable current sprint.
  - heading "Build" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Move implementation forward against the current sprint while keeping the docs aligned with reality.
  - heading "Adjust" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Handle requirement changes explicitly instead of letting them silently alter the project direction.
  - heading "Ship" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Review whether the current increment is actually complete and whether the handoff or release state is honest.

  - heading "How to use it" [level=2]
  - paragraph: This repository makes the most sense when you treat it as an operating repo, not just a folder of documents.
  - list:
    - text: Read
    - code: README.md
    - text: to understand the repository’s role and workflow.
    - text: Read
    - code: SKILL.md
    - text: to see how the assistant is expected to behave.
    - text: Read
    - code: AGENTS.md
    - text: and the current core docs to understand the current product state.
    - listitem: If the product is still undefined, ask what should be built before starting major implementation.
    - listitem: "Update the baseline docs first: project seed, brief, functional spec, roadmap, backlog, current sprint, and done definition."
    - text: Proceed with implementation against

    - code: change-requests.md
    - text: and the source-of-truth docs before changing direction.
  - paragraph: If you only want the fastest introduction, start with the README and the worked static-tool example. If you want to use it seriously, go through the validation scripts and bootstrap helper as well.
  - heading "Bootstrap helper" [level=2]
  - paragraph: "If you want starter docs for a new product idea, the repository includes a helper script:"
  - code: python3 scripts/bootstrap_new_product.py "Your Product Name" --one-line "One-line description" --user "target user"
  - paragraph: This generates starter files for a seed, brief, functional spec, roadmap, current sprint, and done definition. It is not a finished-product generator. It gives you a usable starting point that still needs real clarification, prioritization, and human review.
  - heading "Why NicheWorks publishes it" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: NicheWorks publishes small, practical tools and workflow assets meant to be useful in real work.
    - code: product-founder-os
    - text: "fits that line as a repository asset for a common operational problem: AI-assisted product work that drifts because the product was never clearly defined or kept current."
  - paragraph: It is not presented as a magic product generator. It is presented as a useful, durable foundation for keeping product work from collapsing into vague sessions, stale docs, and fake completion.
  - heading "FAQ" [level=2]
  - heading "Is Product Founder OS just a prompt collection?" [level=3]
  - paragraph: No. It is a repository operating system built around README, SKILL, AGENTS, core docs, examples, and helper scripts.
  - heading "Can I use it with GPT only?" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Yes. Product definition and planning work can be done with GPT alone. Codex becomes especially useful when repository editing and implementation need to continue from the same structure.
  - heading "Does bootstrap_new_product.py generate a finished product?" [level=3]
  - paragraph: No. It generates starter docs only. The result still needs clarification, planning, and human review.
  - heading "Does this repository guarantee launch success?" [level=3]
  - paragraph: No. It provides structure and workflow discipline, not product-market fit, legal guarantees, or security guarantees.

  - heading "What it is" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Release Guardian is a practical release-preflight repository asset for Codex-style repository work. It is designed for the final pass before launch, when a project may technically run but still be weak as a public release.
  - paragraph:
    - text: Typical problems at that stage include missing title or description metadata, missing crawl files, weak public-facing basics, accidental
    - code: noindex
    - text: ", README drift, unclear deploy assumptions, or a vague sense that a repo is “probably ready” without a structured verdict."
  - paragraph: "This repository exists to turn that vague final pass into a repeatable workflow: inspect the repo, run safe checks, classify blockers vs warnings, optionally apply only narrow low-risk fixes, and return a consistent release-readiness result."
  - heading "Who it is for" [level=2]
  - paragraph: This project is a good fit for people shipping public-facing repositories and wanting a more disciplined last-mile release check. It is especially useful if you work inside real repositories instead of abstract examples and want a practical release verdict with explicit boundaries.
  - list:
    - listitem: Individual builders shipping small web tools or public utility repos.
    - listitem: People using Codex or agent-assisted repository workflows.
    - listitem: Maintainers who want a cleaner ship / no-ship style check.
    - listitem: Teams that want narrow safe-fix behavior instead of broad automatic edits.
    - listitem: Anyone who wants practical release basics to be explicit, not improvised.
  - paragraph: It is a worse fit if you are looking for a full security audit suite, legal review system, accessibility audit, privacy audit, infrastructure governance framework, or autonomous release bot.
  - heading "What it checks" [level=2]
  - paragraph: The current repository focuses on practical public-release basics for web repositories.
  - heading "Universal checks" [level=3]
  - list:
    - listitem: README presence and clarity
    - listitem: LICENSE presence
    - listitem: favicon presence
    - listitem: title and meta description
    - listitem: OGP and social metadata basics
    - listitem: canonical basics
    - code: robots.txt
    - code: sitemap.xml
    - listitem: 404 handling
    - text: accidental
    - code: noindex
    - listitem: obvious docs drift
    - listitem: public-facing support, contact, and disclaimer basics
  - heading "Framework-oriented checks" [level=3]
  - paragraph: The implementation can inspect common public web-app shapes including static HTML repos, Vite-style repos, React-style repos, and Next.js-like metadata entry structures.
  - heading "Release-readiness checks" [level=3]
  - paragraph: When repo-defined scripts exist, the CLI can run practical checks such as build, lint, typecheck, and test, then classify the results as blockers or warnings.
  - heading "Modes" [level=2]
  - strong: 1. Report-only
  - text: Inspect the repository, run safe checks when appropriate, and report findings without editing files.
  - strong: 2. Safe-fix
  - text: Apply only narrow, low-risk corrections such as missing meta description stable contents, favicon references, robots.txt, and sitemap.xml scaffolds. Review the findings first and always inspect the resulting diff.
  - strong: 3. Blocker-first
  - text: Focus only on the issues most likely to stop or delay launch, and stop early when a serious blocker has already been confirmed.
  - strong: 4. Release-report
  - text: Return a clean, handoff-friendly report shape for PR comments, issues, release notes, or launch review.

  - paragraph: The repository is organized as a practical, reusable package rather than a single prompt file.

  - heading "Glossary" [level=2]
  - term: release-preflight
  - definition: A practical pre-launch check before publishing a repository or web project.
  - term: safe-fix
  - definition: A narrow automatic fix mode intended for limited low-risk release basics. It still requires diff review.
  - term: blocker
  - definition: A serious issue that should stop or delay release until fixed.
  - term: warning
  - definition: An issue that may not block release but should be reviewed before shipping.
  - term: verdict
  - definition: The final structured judgment produced by the workflow.
  - heading "Why NicheWorks publishes it" [level=2]
  - paragraph: "NicheWorks publishes small, practical tools and workflow assets that are meant to be used in real work. Release Guardian fits that model: it is a narrowly scoped repository asset for a real operational problem, the rushed and inconsistent final pass before shipping."
  - paragraph: It is not positioned as a magic auditor. It is positioned as a useful working asset that can keep improving through better examples, better tests, and tighter release discipline over time.
  - heading "FAQ" [level=2]
  - heading "Is Release Guardian just a checklist?" [level=3]
  - paragraph: No. It is built as a Codex-native repository asset with operational instructions, helper scripts, templates, and self-tests, not only as a static checklist.
  - heading "What should I do before running safe-fix?" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Commit or stash current changes, run report-only first, use safe-fix only after reviewing findings, and review git diff after safe-fix.
  - heading "Can it guarantee a successful release?" [level=3]
  - paragraph: No. It checks practical preflight signals and returns a structured verdict, but final release decisions still need human review.
  - heading "Can I run it on private repositories?" [level=3]
  - paragraph: You can, but check what reports, logs, or generated outputs may contain before sharing them outside your trusted environment.
  - heading "Is this a security audit tool?" [level=3]
  - paragraph: No. It is a release-preflight helper, not a security, legal, accessibility, privacy, or compliance audit.
